### INFP and ISTP: the same task, two kinds of material and two standards

In a fictional project, two colleagues receive the same examples, goal, and deadline. Both can consider which options meet common evaluation criteria and which features matter to the intended users.

The colleagues can also use different kinds of information. One approach checks what the examples document. Another looks for patterns across the same examples and asks what else might work. The contrast illustrates S/N.

A proposal that serves a purpose still needs to work under the actual conditions. A proposal that meets the technical criteria still needs a purpose. Both checks can inform the decision.

An ISTP can ask what a proposal means to the people affected. An INFP can check measurements. Experience and responsibility can explain which questions they ask. The order cannot establish type.

### INFP and ISTP: why not one function overlaps

In type dynamics, P points to an outward-facing perceiving process. With I, it is auxiliary: extraverted Intuition (Ne) for INFP and extraverted Sensing (Se) for ISTP. Their inward-facing dominant processes are introverted Feeling (Fi) and introverted Thinking (Ti), respectively.

The notation used here gives INFP Fi–Ne–Si–Te and ISTP Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. At each corresponding position, the process differs: Fi/Ti, Ne/Se, Si/Ni, and Te/Fe. Both stacks follow the same inward–outward pattern in this convention.

The Foundation lists tertiary Sensing for INFP (Se or Si) and tertiary Intuition for ISTP (Ne or Ni). We use Si and Ni. Choosing the alternatives would leave the first two positions unchanged but introduce overlap with the other type’s auxiliary process. comparison.summary:
INFP and ISTP share Introversion (I) and Perceiving (P). They differ on Sensing/Intuition and Thinking/Feeling. S/N concerns what information they give weight to. T/F concerns how they make decisions.

- **I (shared):** Introversion describes attention and energy directed more toward inner ideas and reflection. It does not measure shyness or how much someone speaks.
- **P (shared):** Perceiving favors keeping options open in dealings with the outside world. Either type can commit to a plan or meet a deadline.
- **S/N:** ISTP’s Sensing emphasizes observable details and relevant experience. INFP’s Intuition emphasizes connections, patterns, and possibilities.
- **T/F:** ISTP’s Thinking emphasizes logical consistency and criteria that can be applied consistently. INFP’s Feeling emphasizes values and how a decision affects people. Either person can consider both.

In the notation used here, INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Each corresponding position contains a different process with the same inward or outward orientation. The Foundation gives alternatives for the tertiary attitudes, so whether the two stacks share a process depends on the notation.

Either type can check facts, explore possibilities, question the reasoning, or consider who might be affected. The order of their actions cannot establish type, skill, or compatibility.

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
All six examples use the same materials, responsibilities, decision authority, and deadline. Either person can consider both approaches. Each row isolates either the information used or the criteria for deciding.

| Same situation, information, and authority | INFP: possible emphasis | ISTP: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Choosing between two feasible proposals | Which one better reflects the values and needs of the people affected? | Which one holds up better when the same criteria are applied to both? | T/F: people and values or consistent evaluation criteria |
| Reviewing examples for a new task | What patterns in the examples suggest about possible approaches | Which conditions, measurements, and results the same examples document | S/N: possible connections and concrete details |
| Deciding how to address a roadblock raised by a colleague | Which response takes the colleague’s situation and the effects on others into account? | Which response meets the same decision criteria when applied to comparable roadblocks? | T/F: consequences for people and consistently applied criteria |
| Choosing between two revisions midway through the work | Which revision better serves the people the work is meant to help? | Which revision follows most consistently from the agreed requirements and evidence? | T/F: impact and values or consistent criteria. Either person can consider both. |
| Choosing what the same handover should explain | Which decisions will matter most to the people receiving the work? | Which decisions need explaining under the same standard used for comparable handovers? | T/F: priorities of the people involved and consistent reporting criteria |
| Reviewing the same collaboration notes afterward | Which connections recur across the notes and what they suggest for future work | Which steps, measurements, and changes the notes record | S/N: possible patterns and documented details. The row does not compare memory. |

An experienced INFP may know which dimension to check. An ISTP joining a project may ask why it matters. Training, responsibilities, and available information can explain what either person does. The table does not determine type.
compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Either type might speak at length about a familiar task or listen quietly in a new setting. Responsibilities, familiarity, and the topic can explain those choices.

Shared I concerns the direction of attention and energy. Shared P concerns keeping options open as new information arrives. Neither tells you how quickly someone will speak or commit.

Ask two separate questions: what information did the person rely on (S/N), and what criteria guided the decision (T/F)? Anyone can check concrete facts and weigh values, or look for patterns and apply consistent criteria.

### INFP and ISTP: the same task, two kinds of material and two standards

In a fictional project, two colleagues receive the same examples, goal, and deadline. Both can consider which options meet common evaluation criteria and which features matter to the intended users.

The colleagues can also use different kinds of information. One approach checks what the examples document. Another looks for patterns across the same examples and asks what else might work. The contrast illustrates S/N.

A proposal that serves a purpose still needs to work under the actual conditions. A proposal that meets the technical criteria still needs a purpose. Both checks can inform the decision.

An ISTP can ask what a proposal means to the people affected. An INFP can check measurements. Experience and responsibility can explain which questions they ask. The order cannot establish type.

### INFP and ISTP: why not one function overlaps

In type dynamics, P points to an outward-facing perceiving process. With I, it is auxiliary: extraverted Intuition (Ne) for INFP and extraverted Sensing (Se) for ISTP. Their inward-facing dominant processes are introverted Feeling (Fi) and introverted Thinking (Ti), respectively.

The notation used here gives INFP Fi–Ne–Si–Te and ISTP Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. At each corresponding position, the process differs: Fi/Ti, Ne/Se, Si/Ni, and Te/Fe. Both stacks follow the same inward–outward pattern in this convention.

The Foundation lists tertiary Sensing for INFP (Se or Si) and tertiary Intuition for ISTP (Ne or Ni). We use Si and Ni. Choosing the alternatives would leave the first two positions unchanged but introduce overlap with the other type’s auxiliary process. See the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Both examples are fictional. Coaching, probation, and promotion should be assessed against the work and the role’s requirements. Either type can use any of the approaches shown.

A team may need a clear purpose and a workable set of steps. Who explains each part can follow from their experience and responsibilities.

### INFP and ISTP: two ways of breaking down the same coaching task

In this fictional training task, two coaches have the same twenty interview transcripts, deadline, and completion criteria. One approach asks the new colleague to identify questions participants would want addressed. Another demonstrates how to group recurring topics and choose passages that support each group.

Using only the first approach can leave the work hard to organize. Using only the second can produce a neatly formatted list that overlooks important concerns. The same coach can use both.

Use the same completion criteria for both approaches. Give the learner a comparable set of transcripts, and ask them to explain their choices and point to supporting passages. This checks the training outcome without using type or speaking time as evidence.

### INFP and ISTP: planning for a flat-pack shelf

In this fictional example, two roommates have the same instructions, parts list, room measurements, and deadline. They want to decide whether the shelf fits their space and what they need to verify before assembly.

One approach checks what the measurements, parts list, and instructions actually say. Another considers possible uses and how the placement might affect them. Either roommate can draw on both kinds of information.

Compare the intended use with the documented requirements. If something is missing or the installation requirements are unclear, check the manufacturer’s guidance or ask a qualified installer. Neither the order of the checks nor who volunteers to help can distinguish the types.

faq_blocks.answer:
Either type can speak at length or stay quiet. INFP and ISTP share Introversion and Perceiving. Their letter differences are S/N and T/F.

Compare the information and criteria someone relied on across choices they had room to make. A single silence, short answer, or order of actions cannot establish type.
faq_blocks.question: Both are quiet — what makes them different?

faq_blocks.answer:
In the notation used here, there is no exact match: INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Corresponding positions share the same inward or outward orientation under this convention.

The Foundation also allows Se for INFP’s tertiary process and Ne for ISTP’s. Those choices can add overlap across positions. The dominant and auxiliary processes remain Fi/Ne for INFP and Ti/Se for ISTP.
faq_blocks.question: How many functions do INFP and ISTP actually share? I have seen other accounts

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. Both can value the purpose of the work and develop the relevant skills. Time spent and speed on one task depend on experience and the work involved.

For reflection, ask what mattered in the decision and what would have changed it. Neither sustained interest nor a fast start determines S/N or T/F.
faq_blocks.question: Can an ISTP care about meaning and an INFP be skilled at repairs?

faq_blocks.answer:
A learner can understand why a task matters and still need to see how it is done. A demonstration can make the steps clear while leaving the learner unsure why to choose them for unfamiliar material.

Explain the purpose, demonstrate the steps, and let the learner justify a choice on a new example. Adjust the sequence to their experience and the time available.
faq_blocks.question: What follows from the two ways of breaking down a coaching task?

faq_blocks.answer:
Either person can offer advice when a friend wants to be heard or reassurance when they want help choosing a next step.

Ask whether the friend wants someone to listen or help consider options. Check again if the conversation changes.
faq_blocks.question: As friends, which kind of help most easily makes things worse?

faq_blocks.answer:
Use several real choices with similar responsibilities and stakes. A task you chose yourself may still have constraints that affected what you did.

Write down the information, decision criteria, and constraints for each example. Use the notes to reflect on your habits rather than to score yourself or infer a type from a hobby.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Either type might speak at length about a familiar task or listen quietly in a new setting. Responsibilities, familiarity, and the topic can explain those choices.

Shared I concerns the direction of attention and energy. Shared P concerns keeping options open as new information arrives. Neither tells you how quickly someone will speak or commit.

Ask two separate questions: what information did the person rely on (S/N), and what criteria guided the decision (T/F)? Anyone can check concrete facts and weigh values, or look for patterns and apply consistent criteria.

### INFP and ISTP: the same task, two kinds of material and two standards

In a fictional project, two colleagues receive the same examples, goal, and deadline. Both can consider which options meet common evaluation criteria and which features matter to the intended users.

The colleagues can also use different kinds of information. One approach checks what the examples document. Another looks for patterns across the same examples and asks what else might work. The contrast illustrates S/N.

A proposal that serves a purpose still needs to work under the actual conditions. A proposal that meets the technical criteria still needs a purpose. Both checks can inform the decision.

An ISTP can ask what a proposal means to the people affected. An INFP can check measurements. Experience and responsibility can explain which questions they ask. The order cannot establish type.

### INFP and ISTP: why not one function overlaps

In type dynamics, P points to an outward-facing perceiving process. With I, it is auxiliary: extraverted Intuition (Ne) for INFP and extraverted Sensing (Se) for ISTP. Their inward-facing dominant processes are introverted Feeling (Fi) and introverted Thinking (Ti), respectively.

The notation used here gives INFP Fi–Ne–Si–Te and ISTP Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. At each corresponding position, the process differs: Fi/Ti, Ne/Se, Si/Ni, and Te/Fe. Both stacks follow the same inward–outward pattern in this convention.

The Foundation lists tertiary Sensing for INFP (Se or Si) and tertiary Intuition for ISTP (Ne or Ni). We use Si and Ni. Choosing the alternatives would leave the first two positions unchanged but introduce overlap with the other type’s auxiliary process. See the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

sections.body_md:
All six examples use the same materials, responsibilities, decision authority, and deadline. Either person can consider both approaches. Each row isolates either the information used or the criteria for deciding.

| Same situation, information, and authority | INFP: possible emphasis | ISTP: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Choosing between two feasible proposals | Which one better reflects the values and needs of the people affected? | Which one holds up better when the same criteria are applied to both? | T/F: people and values or consistent evaluation criteria |
| Reviewing examples for a new task | What patterns in the examples suggest about possible approaches | Which conditions, measurements, and results the same examples document | S/N: possible connections and concrete details |
| Deciding how to address a roadblock raised by a colleague | Which response takes the colleague’s situation and the effects on others into account? | Which response meets the same decision criteria when applied to comparable roadblocks? | T/F: consequences for people and consistently applied criteria |
| Choosing between two revisions midway through the work | Which revision better serves the people the work is meant to help? | Which revision follows most consistently from the agreed requirements and evidence? | T/F: impact and values or consistent criteria. Either person can consider both. |
| Choosing what the same handover should explain | Which decisions will matter most to the people receiving the work? | Which decisions need explaining under the same standard used for comparable handovers? | T/F: priorities of the people involved and consistent reporting criteria |
| Reviewing the same collaboration notes afterward | Which connections recur across the notes and what they suggest for future work | Which steps, measurements, and changes the notes record | S/N: possible patterns and documented details. The row does not compare memory. |

An experienced INFP may know which dimension to check. An ISTP joining a project may ask why it matters. Training, responsibilities, and available information can explain what either person does. The table does not determine type.
sections.title: INFP and ISTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Both examples are fictional. Coaching, probation, and promotion should be assessed against the work and the role’s requirements. Either type can use any of the approaches shown.

A team may need a clear purpose and a workable set of steps. Who explains each part can follow from their experience and responsibilities.

### INFP and ISTP: two ways of breaking down the same coaching task

In this fictional training task, two coaches have the same twenty interview transcripts, deadline, and completion criteria. One approach asks the new colleague to identify questions participants would want addressed. Another demonstrates how to group recurring topics and choose passages that support each group.

Using only the first approach can leave the work hard to organize. Using only the second can produce a neatly formatted list that overlooks important concerns. The same coach can use both.

Use the same completion criteria for both approaches. Give the learner a comparable set of transcripts, and ask them to explain their choices and point to supporting passages. This checks the training outcome without using type or speaking time as evidence.

### INFP and ISTP: planning for a flat-pack shelf

In this fictional example, two roommates have the same instructions, parts list, room measurements, and deadline. They want to decide whether the shelf fits their space and what they need to verify before assembly.

One approach checks what the measurements, parts list, and instructions actually say. Another considers possible uses and how the placement might affect them. Either roommate can draw on both kinds of information.

Compare the intended use with the documented requirements. If something is missing or the installation requirements are unclear, check the manufacturer’s guidance or ask a qualified installer. Neither the order of the checks nor who volunteers to help can distinguish the types.

sections.body_md:
Silence can reflect concentration, uncertainty, pressure, or the setting. Either person may have a lot to say about a familiar subject. Speaking time and order tell you little about S/N or T/F.

Hobbies and occupations reflect a person’s interests, access, and experience. Drawing, repairing things, and playing music do not identify a type.

Thinking and Feeling describe which criteria carry weight. Either person can consider whether a proposal works and what it means for the people affected. Neither preference measures realism or compassion.

Role, experience, deadline, and available information can explain whether someone measures the space or discusses its use first. The order cannot establish a preference.

sections.body_md:
Compare the assessment, version, language, and scoring guidance. Consider which situations you had in mind. Work can shape which examples are familiar without establishing a predictable direction for the score.

Recall several comparable decisions where you had room to choose. Record which information you used, what criteria guided your decision, and how responsibilities or deadlines affected it. Separate facts and patterns (S/N) from criteria and effects on people (T/F).

Include cases where you took a different approach and note what changed. Use the records for reflection. They do not produce a score or determine your type.

items.answer:
Either type can speak at length or stay quiet. INFP and ISTP share Introversion and Perceiving. Their letter differences are S/N and T/F.

Compare the information and criteria someone relied on across choices they had room to make. A single silence, short answer, or order of actions cannot establish type.
items.question: Both are quiet — what makes them different?

items.answer:
In the notation used here, there is no exact match: INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Corresponding positions share the same inward or outward orientation under this convention.

The Foundation also allows Se for INFP’s tertiary process and Ne for ISTP’s. Those choices can add overlap across positions. The dominant and auxiliary processes remain Fi/Ne for INFP and Ti/Se for ISTP.
items.question: How many functions do INFP and ISTP actually share? I have seen other accounts

items.answer:
Yes. Both can value the purpose of the work and develop the relevant skills. Time spent and speed on one task depend on experience and the work involved.

For reflection, ask what mattered in the decision and what would have changed it. Neither sustained interest nor a fast start determines S/N or T/F.
items.question: Can an ISTP care about meaning and an INFP be skilled at repairs?

items.answer:
A learner can understand why a task matters and still need to see how it is done. A demonstration can make the steps clear while leaving the learner unsure why to choose them for unfamiliar material.

Explain the purpose, demonstrate the steps, and let the learner justify a choice on a new example. Adjust the sequence to their experience and the time available.
items.question: What follows from the two ways of breaking down a coaching task?

items.answer:
Either person can offer advice when a friend wants to be heard or reassurance when they want help choosing a next step.

Ask whether the friend wants someone to listen or help consider options. Check again if the conversation changes.
items.question: As friends, which kind of help most easily makes things worse?

items.answer:
Use several real choices with similar responsibilities and stakes. A task you chose yourself may still have constraints that affected what you did.

Write down the information, decision criteria, and constraints for each example. Use the notes to reflect on your habits rather than to score yourself or infer a type from a hobby.
